summaries.example: Imagine a garden where some plants make seeds that are very much like themselves. The seeds are copies, but the plants and soil help make those copies. In this picture, the seed-making pattern is like a replicator, while the whole plant is more like a vehicle: it interacts with the world and helps the pattern continue.
summaries.summary: This entry asks what replication is and why it matters for evolution. A replicator is something whose pattern is copied. Genes are the best-known biological example, but the entry explains that the word can be used more broadly. Richard Dawkins separates replicators from vehicles. Replicators are copied, while vehicles interact with the environment in ways that help copying succeed. David Hull proposed the related idea of an interactor, which emphasizes active cause-and-effect rather than a passive container. The entry also discusses possible replicators in immune responses, culture, and developmental systems. Some researchers think that genes should not have a special place in every explanation of inheritance. Others argue that natural selection can occur without high-fidelity copying, as long as there is variation, differences in success, and some inheritance. The main lesson is that replication is a useful way to understand evolution, but it may not be required in every case.
key_ideas: Genes are often treated as biological replicators because DNA can be copied and passed through generations.
A replicator and a vehicle have different jobs: one is copied, while the other interacts with the environment.
Some philosophers and scientists think copying is not required for natural selection; resemblance between parents and offspring may be enough.
The idea of replicators has been extended to culture, development, and other systems, but these extensions are debated.
summaries.why_it_matters: The idea of replication helps us understand how traits can continue across generations. It also helps us ask careful questions about genes, organisms, culture, and learning. The topic matters because a simple word like “copy” can hide many different processes. Studying those differences can show why scientists and philosophers sometimes disagree about what evolution needs.

important_terms.definition: A thing or pattern that makes copies of itself, or whose copies are made and passed on.
An entity that helps a replicator survive and make more copies by interacting with its surroundings.
A process in which living things with different traits leave different numbers of descendants, and those traits can be passed on.
The instructions or pattern carried in something, such as the sequence in DNA.
A feature that makes an organism or other entity better suited to its surroundings.

questions_to_think_about: Does something have to make an exact copy to count as a replicator?
Can a plant, animal, or group help copying happen without being the thing that is copied?
Could natural selection happen when children only partly resemble their parents?
What might be gained or lost by comparing cultural change with biological evolution?

summaries.example: Consider two populations of simple organisms that differ in size. Larger organisms leave more descendants, but their offspring only partly resemble them. If size is still inherited enough that larger parents tend, on average, to have larger offspring, the average size can increase over generations. This illustrates the classical recipe for natural selection—variation, differences in fitness, and heritability—without requiring high-fidelity replication.
summaries.summary: The entry examines whether replication is essential to reproduction and evolution by natural selection. Modern discussions often describe genes in informational terms, but the source stresses that “information” has several competing meanings. A physically grounded interpretation concerns the way molecular sequences specify other sequences or protein structures; broader informational language can make genes seem abstract and transferable across biological, cultural, or computational domains. Dawkins introduced replicators as a more general category than genes. On his account, replicators are copied entities whose persistence, multiplication, and copying accuracy affect evolutionary change, while vehicles are the entities that interact with environments and help replicators spread. Hull’s interactor concept redirects attention to causal environmental activity and avoids assuming that every replicator is housed in an organism. The entry then considers immune-system responses, cultural transmission, and extended replicators that include non-genetic developmental resources. Critics associated with developmental-systems approaches deny that genes have an automatically privileged role in producing inherited traits. A different challenge comes from the classical population-level account of selection: variation, differential fitness, and positive heritability can produce evolutionary change even when offspring are not precise copies. The source therefore treats replication as a powerful heuristic, not an unquestionable foundation. It also discusses the possibility that replicators themselves arose through earlier selection among entities that merely persisted or multiplied, and compares replicators with broader notions of reproducers.
key_ideas: Dawkins generalizes from genes to replicators and distinguishes the copied entity from the entity that interacts with the environment.
Replicators are often described through longevity, fecundity, and copy-fidelity, though these properties raise questions about whether the relevant unit is a physical object or an inherited type.
Hull’s notion of an interactor broadens the analysis by emphasizing causal environmental interaction rather than treating vehicles as mere containers.

The classical account of natural selection requires variation, fitness differences, and heritability, not necessarily replication; the replicator account may describe a particularly clear or “pure” case.

Developmental-systems theorists challenge the special status sometimes given to genes, while extended-replicator views include non-genetic resources such as stable habitats, learned behaviors, or social transmission.
Cultural evolution and immune responses may show selection-like patterns, but whether they involve replicators in the same sense as genes remains contested.
summaries.why_it_matters: Replication is a bridge between molecular biology and general evolutionary theory. It lets researchers compare genes with cultural patterns, immune-system variants, or developmental resources, while also forcing them to ask whether those comparisons are scientifically justified. The debate clarifies the difference between copying, reproduction, inheritance, persistence, and selection. It also warns against turning a useful abstraction into the claim that every evolutionary process must have the same structure as gene-based evolution.

important_terms.definition: An entity or pattern whose copies are produced and whose persistence through copying can affect evolutionary change; Dawkins uses the term more generally than “gene.”
Hull’s term for an entity that interacts causally with its environment in a way that affects the reproduction or persistence of relevant replicators.
Dawkins’s term for entities associated with replicators that aid their persistence through environmental interaction; critics argue that it can suggest an overly passive role.
The tendency for offspring to resemble parents in a relevant trait; it can be positive without being perfect copying.
A population-level process involving variation, differences in reproductive or persistence success, and the transmission of relevant differences.
The view that development results from the coordinated contributions of genes, organisms, environments, and other resources, without automatically granting genes a privileged causal role.

questions_to_think_about: Is high-fidelity copying a necessary condition for natural selection, or only especially useful for explaining it?
Should a general theory of selection focus on replicators, interactors, populations, or developmental systems?
When does a cultural pattern count as a replicator rather than a recurring or attractive idea?
Does treating genes as information clarify biology, or can it hide the material mechanisms that make inheritance possible?
How should we choose the level of description at which two entities count as copies?

summaries.example: Suppose students teach one another a basketball move. The move may spread through demonstrations, videos, conversations, and practice. Each learner may change it slightly, so it is not copied as exactly as a DNA sequence. One view might call the transmitted pattern a cultural replicator, with brains, books, or videos acting as vehicles. Critics may instead say that the important facts are variation, which versions spread more, and how much of each version is inherited through learning.
summaries.summary: “Replication” can mean making copies, but the entry shows that evolutionary theory uses the idea in several connected ways. Genes are familiar biological examples, yet Richard Dawkins introduced “replicator” as a broader term for entities or patterns whose copying affects their evolutionary success. His framework separates replicators from vehicles: replicators are copied, whereas vehicles interact with environments in ways that help the replicators persist. David Hull replaces the passive-sounding vehicle with “interactor,” stressing that selection depends on causal activity at several possible levels. The entry also examines what biologists mean by information. DNA sequences physically participate in molecular processes, but treating genes as abstract information can make the same evolutionary framework seem applicable to culture or other domains. This generality is useful, but it may also hide the material mechanisms that connect inherited patterns to organisms. Cultural transmission is sometimes described using memes, though cultural patterns may have less stable boundaries and lower copying fidelity than genes. Developmental-systems theorists further challenge the assumption that genes alone carry the important inherited information. Finally, the entry presents a population-level alternative: natural selection may require variation, differences in fitness, and heritability, without requiring exact replication. Replication may represent a particularly clear case of inheritance, rather than an indispensable condition of every selective process. The source also explores how selection might have produced replicators from earlier entities that simply persisted or multiplied.
key_ideas: The word “replicator” was introduced to describe copying more generally than the word “gene.”
Dawkins gives genes a central role in biological replication, while Hull’s interactors emphasize active causal relations with the environment.
A copy can remain similar in relevant ways without being identical in every detail, which makes the level of description important.
Some accounts apply replicator ideas to culture, immune responses, and developmental inheritance, but the analogies are disputed.
A population can evolve by natural selection with imperfect inheritance if variation and differences in success are present.
The entry considers whether replication was an original starting point of evolution or an outcome of earlier selection for persistence and multiplication.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate teaches us how scientific concepts can be broadened—and what can go wrong when an analogy is stretched too far. Replicator language connects genetics with questions about culture, development, and the origin of life, but different systems may differ in important ways. Understanding those differences helps students evaluate claims about “selfish” genes, cultural transmission, and the requirements of natural selection without assuming that one model settles every case.

important_terms.definition: A thing or pattern that is copied across generations or transmission events and can become more or less common.
A thing that interacts with its surroundings in a way that affects which replicators become more common.
Dawkins’s name for an entity that carries or supports replicators while interacting with the environment.
The passing on of a trait or pattern so that descendants tend to resemble earlier members, even if the resemblance is imperfect.
Evolutionary change produced when populations vary, some variants do better, and relevant differences are passed on.
The idea that development depends on many resources, not genes alone, and that no one resource must always have the leading causal role.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a philosopher prefer the broader word “replicator” to the narrower word “gene”?
Are memes useful scientific entities, or do cultural patterns change too much to behave like genes?
What is the difference between an entity being copied and an entity helping copies spread?
Could selection favor something that lasts longer even if it produces no offspring?
How might a developmental-systems view change the way we explain inherited traits?
